issues.name: Governing law – UCC Article 2 / merchants
issues.rule: UCC Article 2 governs contracts for the sale of goods (movable things); merchant status (regular dealing in goods of the kind) triggers merchant rules such as good faith as honesty plus commercial reasonableness.
keyFacts: Seller sells imported food products to local food distributors like Buyer
2,500 pounds of Canadian wild rice
issues.analysis: Wild rice is a good, so Article 2 applies, and both Seller and Buyer are food merchants. Writing was stated to be valid, so the Statute of Frauds (goods over $500) is satisfied and is not a real issue.

issues.name: Third-party beneficiary – intended donee beneficiary
issues.rule: A non-party may enforce a contract if it is an intended beneficiary (Restatement 2d s.302): recognizing the beneficiary's right is appropriate to effectuate the parties' intent, and either the performance satisfies a money debt or the promisee intends to give the beneficiary the benefit of the promised performance (donee beneficiary). Incidental beneficiaries have no rights.
keyFacts: Seller agrees to deliver free of any charge an additional 200 pounds of the identical product to Food Bank
Buyer ... insisted on a provision
issues.analysis: Food Bank is expressly named in the contract and Buyer, the promisee, insisted on the gift, so it is an intended donee beneficiary with standing to enforce the promise to deliver 200 pounds.

issues.name: Third-party beneficiary – vesting of rights
issues.rule: An intended beneficiary's rights vest, and can no longer be modified or rescinded by the original parties, when the beneficiary manifests assent, sues, or materially changes position in justifiable reliance on the promise (Restatement 2d s.311).
keyFacts: Immediately after Buyer informed Food Bank
Food Bank spent $300 for 200 one-pound bags
labeled 'Famous Canadian Wild Rice'
issues.analysis: Food Bank learned of the promise and spent $300 on labeled bags and planned a campaign, a material, foreseeable change of position, so its rights vested and Buyer and Seller could not discharge them by terminating. Student B's reliance on UCC merchant additional-terms (s.2-207) is misplaced because the term was in the signed original contract, not an additional term in an acceptance.

issues.name: Seller's breach – perfect tender and cure
issues.rule: UCC 2-601 perfect tender: buyer may reject goods or the tender if it fails in any respect to conform to the contract. Seller may cure under 2-508 if time for performance has not expired, or if it had reasonable grounds to believe the tender would be acceptable and seasonably notifies buyer. Buyer must reject within a reasonable time with seasonable notice specifying defects (2-602, 2-605), and must act in good faith (1-304).
keyFacts: packed in 100-pound sacks
packed in 50-kilogram sacks that contained 110.2 pounds each
Buyer refused to accept the delivery
Seller believes Buyer refused ... because Buyer had found a cheaper source
issues.analysis: The 110.2-pound sacks technically fail the 100-pound-sack term, so Buyer could reject under perfect tender; total weight was correct and the deviation is trivial, so Seller will argue Buyer's pretextual rejection was bad faith and that it may cure (it delivered on the last day, 'on or before May 1', so 2-508(1) is likely unavailable, 2-508(2) is arguable). Close call, but likely a rightful though possibly pretextual rejection; Buyer's fax gave only a general reason (2-605 issue).

issues.name: Seller's defenses – impossibility / impracticability / frustration
issues.rule: Under UCC 2-615 performance is excused only if made impracticable by a contingency whose nonoccurrence was a basic assumption of the contract; increased cost alone, or a foreseeable and seller-controlled supplier change, is not enough. Frustration of purpose requires the supervening event to destroy the value of the contract for a party and be unforeseen.
keyFacts: his Canadian producer had recently switched to metric weights
Seller's agent explained
issues.analysis: Seller could have re-bagged or sourced 100-pound sacks at modest cost; a supplier's packaging change is a risk Seller bore, so these defenses fail. Frustration is inapposite because Buyer's rejection, not a supervening event, caused the problem.

issues.name: Seller's defenses – Buyer's breach / wrongful rejection / repudiation
issues.rule: A buyer who wrongfully rejects or repudiates (2-610) is in breach; a termination without right is a repudiation, and a beneficiary's vested rights remain enforceable against the promisor, who may assert defenses it has against the promisee.
keyFacts: I hereby terminate our purchase agreement
Buyer purchased 2,500 pounds ... from another supplier for $4.00 per pound
issues.analysis: If the nonconformity was trivial or curable and Buyer was acting on price, Seller will argue Buyer breached; but Seller as promisor still must deliver to Food Bank, and Buyer's termination cannot impair Food Bank's vested rights. Seller can assert against Food Bank any defense good against Buyer.

issues.name: Food Bank's remedies – expectation and reliance
issues.rule: A buyer/beneficiary may recover damages for nondelivery (2-713: market price minus contract price, or cover damages under 2-712) plus incidental damages; reliance damages are an alternative measure for expenses incurred in justifiable reliance.
keyFacts: 200 pounds of the identical product ... free of any charge
Food Bank spent $300
Buyer purchased ... for $4.00 per pound
issues.analysis: Food Bank can recover the market value of 200 pounds of rice (market apparently around $4/lb, about $800) plus incidentals, or alternatively its $300 reliance expenditure, but not both for the same loss.

issues.name: Food Bank's remedies – consequential/lost fundraising and mitigation
issues.rule: Consequential damages (2-715(2)) require losses resulting from general or particular requirements of which the seller had reason to know at contracting, reasonable certainty, and inability to prevent by cover or otherwise (mitigation).
keyFacts: believing that the campaign would raise $10,000
Food Bank was unable to find any other affordable source and had to suspend the fundraising effort
issues.analysis: Nothing shows Seller knew of the fundraising plan when contracting and $10,000 of donations is speculative, so consequential damages are unlikely; Food Bank's failure to find an affordable substitute shows reasonable mitigation efforts.

issues.name: Food Bank's remedies – specific performance
issues.rule: Under UCC 2-716 specific performance is available where goods are unique or in other proper circumstances, including inability to cover; equity requires inadequacy of the legal remedy.
keyFacts: Food Bank was unable to find any other affordable source
issues.analysis: Wild rice is fungible and damages are measurable, but Food Bank's inability to cover on affordable terms gives a colorable 2-716 argument; court likely denies given adequate damages. Close call.

notes: Cure under 2-508 and whether rejection was effective are arguable. Both students leaned on perfect tender without addressing cure or good-faith rejection; Student B's 2-207 merchant additional terms analysis is a misapplication. Consider whether examiners expected Seller defenses to be mainly no breach by Seller / Buyer's bad faith plus impracticability.

issues.name: Legal malpractice – duty and scope of representation
issues.rule: An attorney who accepts a client owes a duty to use the skill, prudence and diligence of a reasonably competent attorney; the scope of the engagement is set by the agreement and conduct, and an attorney who undertakes a matter must act competently on it.
keyFacts: Carole hired Larry, a lawyer, to negotiate with her health insurer
Larry suggested filing a claim against Swim Wonder ... Carole agreed
issues.analysis: The original hire was only for the insurer dispute, but Larry himself suggested the Swim Wonder claim and Carole agreed, creating an attorney-client relationship and a duty as to that claim (or at least a duty to advise of the limitations deadline or decline). Larry may argue limited scope; weak.

issues.name: Breach – failure to file or calendar statute of limitations
issues.rule: Failing to file suit within the limitations period, or to advise the client of the deadline, falls below the standard of care of a reasonable attorney; no expert is needed for such an obvious lapse.
keyFacts: In July 2015, Carole broke her neck
In September 2016, Carole hired Larry
In September 2017 ... Larry ... recently learned that her claim was barred by the two-year statute of limitations
issues.analysis: The injury occurred July 2015, so the two-year period ran in July 2017; Larry had about 10 months after being retained and let it lapse while not checking the deadline or keeping Carole informed. Clear breach.

issues.name: Causation – case within a case (underlying claim must have been viable)
issues.rule: In malpractice the plaintiff must prove actual and proximate cause: that but for the attorney's negligence she would have obtained a better result in the underlying matter (she would have won against Swim Wonder and collected).
keyFacts: negligence in its design of the pool
dove into a swimming pool ... struck the bottom
issues.analysis: Carole must prove the merits of a design-defect/negligence/strict-liability claim against Swim Wonder (consumer expectations or risk-utility test; foreseeability of diving injuries) and that it was collectible. Facts are thin; the pool-diving risk is arguably open and obvious and Carole's own comparative fault could reduce recovery. The claim is plausible but uncertain; a close call.

issues.name: Underlying claim – products liability theories
issues.rule: Manufacturers are liable in strict liability for defective products (manufacturing, design, warning) that cause injury, and in negligence for unreasonable design; design defect is shown by consumer-expectation or risk-utility analysis with a feasible safer alternative.
keyFacts: pool manufactured by Swim Wonder
negligence in its design of the pool
issues.analysis: No facts show manufacturing or warning defect; only a design theory is suggested, and its success depends on safer feasible designs (depth markings, shape). This feeds the causation element above.

issues.name: Defenses – comparative fault and assumption of risk (Carole's own conduct)
issues.rule: Plaintiff's comparative negligence reduces damages (pure comparative in California); express or implied assumption of risk may bar or reduce recovery. In malpractice, a client who reasonably relies on her attorney is not negligent for failing to monitor the deadline.
keyFacts: Carole, who had heard nothing about the negligence claim, contacted Larry
In September 2016, Carole hired Larry
issues.analysis: Larry may argue Carole waited 14 months to hire him and another year before inquiring, but a client is entitled to rely on her attorney; little fault attributable. Also relevant to reducing the underlying recovery (she dove into a pool).

issues.name: Damages – measure in legal malpractice
issues.rule: The plaintiff recovers what she would have recovered in the underlying case (economic and noneconomic damages, less amounts attributable to her own comparative fault and collectibility) proximately caused by the malpractice; no windfall, and punitive damages are not available absent malice.
keyFacts: broke her neck and became disabled
her health insurer, which was slow in paying her medical bills
issues.analysis: Carole recovers the judgment she would have obtained from Swim Wonder: medical expenses (past and future), lost earnings, and pain and suffering, reduced by her comparative fault and collectibility, minus attorney fees she would have owed. Fees of the malpractice suit itself are generally not recoverable.

notes: Malpractice statute of limitations (CCP 340.6: one year from discovery) is not raised by the facts or students; Carole sued after Sept 2017 discovery so presumably timely. Student A wrongly suggests tolling for incapacity may apply; California does not toll for physical disability.

issues.name: Governing law and formation – common law services contract; Statute of Frauds
issues.rule: Common law governs service contracts. Contract formation needs offer, acceptance and consideration. A contract performable within one year does not fall within the Statute of Frauds, so no signed writing is needed.
keyFacts: offered to pay Brad $10,000 to paint Alex's cottage
within the next 30 days
Brad then agreed orally
Alex never signed the contract
issues.analysis: A painting contract is a services contract governed by common law; a valid agreement was formed and, because it is to be performed in 30 days, the Statute of Frauds does not apply. Student B incorrectly treats the Statute as an issue because of Alex's lack of signature.

issues.name: Parol evidence / interpretation – 'one coat' statement and terms of the writing
issues.rule: A fully integrated writing may not be contradicted by prior agreements; evidence can explain or interpret ambiguous terms, and prior statements that are not part of the bargain are not terms. Implied terms: a service provider owes performance in a workmanlike manner consistent with trade custom.
keyFacts: the reason that I always get my cottage painted every 5 years is that it has always only needed one coat of paint
The contract did not specify how many coats of paint would be needed
issues.analysis: Brad will use the statement to argue the deal contemplated only one coat; Alex made no promise about coats, only a statement about history, and the writing's silence plus the purpose (a painted cottage) implies whatever coats are needed for a proper paint job. Brad, a professional, bore the risk. The statement is likely admissible background but not a term limiting Brad to one coat.

issues.name: Brad's arguments to avoid/reform – mutual mistake, unilateral mistake, misrepresentation
issues.rule: Mutual mistake as to a basic assumption, material, and not borne by the party, makes a contract voidable; unilateral mistake requires the other party's knowledge or fault; misrepresentation must be false, material, relied on and fraudulent or material and justifiably relied on. A party who bears the risk of mistake (assumed or by trade expertise) cannot avoid.
keyFacts: it has always only needed one coat of paint
Brad paints houses for a living and had seen Alex's cottage
issues.analysis: The statement was true as to the past (the cottage previously needed one coat), no scienter is shown, and Brad is an expert who could have inspected, so he bore the risk; mistake and misrepresentation theories are weak. Student A's suggestion that Brad wins by voiding the contract is unconvincing.

issues.name: Performance – substantial performance vs. material breach by Brad
issues.rule: Constructive conditions: a party who substantially performs can recover the contract price less damages for deviations; one who materially breaches cannot recover on the contract (but may get restitution). Substantial performance considers benefit conferred, cost to cure, and good faith.
keyFacts: the wood had soaked up the first coat of paint, so the cottage looked unpainted and terrible
The cottage would have looked fine with one more coat of paint
Brad painted the cottage in one week
issues.analysis: The job was timely but the cottage looked unpainted, so Brad did not deliver the essential benefit; one more coat would fix it at $7,500 (75% of price), so substantial performance is doubtful, though Brad will argue he did the work Alex described. Likely material breach, or at best substantial performance with a large cost-to-complete offset.

issues.name: Brad's demand for extra $10,000 – pre-existing duty rule / repudiation / bad faith
issues.rule: A promise to do what one is already obligated to do is not consideration for a modification; a demand for more money as a condition of performing is an anticipatory repudiation or breach of good faith, letting the other party cover.
keyFacts: Brad demanded $10,000 for his work and refused to add another coat of paint unless Alex paid another $10,000
issues.analysis: Brad was already obligated to paint the cottage adequately, so his demand is unenforceable as a modification and amounts to a refusal to perform, entitling Alex to treat it as repudiation and to cover with Charles.

issues.name: Alex's remedies – cover / cost of completion and counterclaim
issues.rule: For defective or incomplete construction/service, the non-breaching party recovers the reasonable cost to complete or repair (unless economic waste), less any unpaid contract price, plus incidental/consequential damages.
keyFacts: Alex then hires Charles who puts the second coat of paint on the cottage for $7,500
Alex files a counterclaim for $7,500
issues.analysis: Alex's damages are $7,500 for completion, but since he has not paid the $10,000 price, his net loss is offset against what he would owe Brad; if Brad is entitled to the price on substantial performance, Alex deducts $7,500 (Brad gets $2,500). The counterclaim does not yield an additional payout beyond offset because he never paid Brad.

issues.name: Brad's remedies – contract damages vs. restitution/quantum meruit
issues.rule: A party in material breach cannot recover on the contract but may recover in restitution for the benefit conferred, limited by the contract price and reduced for damages caused; a willful breacher's restitution may be limited.
keyFacts: Brad painted the cottage in one week
Alex is unhappy and refuses to pay Brad anything
issues.analysis: If not substantial performance, Brad can seek the reasonable value of the first coat (likely at most about $2,500, i.e. $10,000 minus the $7,500 to finish); if substantial performance, same net number via contract. Likely outcome: Brad recovers about $2,500 and Alex's counterclaim is offset/denied as a separate recovery.

notes: The outcome is a judgment call (Brad nets $2,500 vs. Brad recovers little and Alex recovers $0 net). Students largely misapplied the Statute of Frauds; neither noted that Alex paid nothing so Alex's counterclaim is only an offset. Student B calls the cottage a barn and mislabels who signed; ignore those slips.

issues.name: Al – conspiracy to commit burglary/larceny
issues.rule: Conspiracy is an agreement between two or more persons with specific intent to achieve an unlawful objective; California and modern law require an overt act by at least one conspirator in furtherance. The conspiracy is complete once agreement plus an overt act occur; each conspirator is guilty of the conspiracy and, under Pinkerton, of foreseeable crimes of co-conspirators in furtherance.
keyFacts: They decide to break into the Gigantic Power Company (GPC) headquarters at night, remove a model
Two hours before ... Al tells Bob and Carl that he will not participate
issues.analysis: The three agreed to burglary (entry into a structure with intent to commit theft) and larceny; if an overt act (planning, preparation) occurred before Al pulled out he can be charged with conspiracy, and if the first overt act (the break-in) occurred only after he withdrew, his conspiracy liability is weaker (arguable). Close call.

issues.name: Al – withdrawal and liability for co-conspirators' later crimes
issues.rule: Withdrawal after the conspiracy has formed is not a defense to conspiracy itself but ends liability for later crimes of co-conspirators if the withdrawing party effectively communicates withdrawal to all members in time for them to abandon the plan (some jurisdictions and MPC also require thwarting). Pinkerton liability covers only reasonably foreseeable crimes in furtherance and committed before withdrawal.
keyFacts: Two hours before they are to leave
Bob and Carl respond that they will go ahead without him
Unknown to Al and Carl, Bob intends to plant a bomb
issues.analysis: Al notified both co-conspirators two hours ahead, so he is not liable for later crimes (bomb, hostage, murder), which also were not foreseeable and outside the agreement's scope. He may remain guilty of conspiracy to burglary/larceny if the agreement and overt act were complete; no accomplice liability since he gave no aid. Student B's claim that withdrawal fails because he did not notify police/thwart reflects MPC-style rules; common law likely suffices.

issues.name: Bob – burglary and larceny (and conspiracy)
issues.rule: Modern/California burglary is entry into a structure with intent to commit larceny or any felony therein; larceny is a trespassory taking and carrying away of another's personal property with intent to permanently deprive. Intent to return or merely display property temporarily negates larceny.
keyFacts: break into the Gigantic Power Company (GPC) headquarters at night
remove a model of a proposed nuclear plant, and hang it in effigy
Bob intends to plant a bomb in the headquarters
issues.analysis: Bob entered a structure at night intending theft (and arson/explosion) so burglary is satisfied; larceny depends on intent to permanently deprive and is arguable because the model was to be hung in effigy (likely they would keep it), plus value. Common-law burglary (dwelling) is not met, so modern law applies. Possible alternative: trespass/vandalism.

issues.name: Bob – attempted arson / bombing (impossibility irrelevant)
issues.rule: Attempt is specific intent to commit the offense plus a direct act beyond mere preparation; arson is malicious burning of a structure (modern statutes include use of explosives). Failure of the device is no defense.
keyFacts: Bob, unseen by Carl, plants a small bomb, which is set to explode at 4:00 a.m.
the bomb fails to explode and is safely disarmed
issues.analysis: Planting and arming a timed bomb is a substantial step; intent to burn or damage the structure is shown, so attempted arson or attempted destruction by explosive. Attempted murder fails because Bob believed the building unoccupied (no intent to kill). Bob's bomb was beyond the scope of the conspiracy, so only Bob is liable.

issues.name: Bob – kidnapping, false imprisonment, assault with deadly weapon
issues.rule: Kidnapping is unlawful movement of a person, by force or threat, against his will for a substantial distance that increases risk of harm (California requires substantial asportation); false imprisonment is unlawful confinement; assault is an attempted battery or intentional creation of reasonable apprehension of imminent harmful contact; aggravated by use of a deadly weapon.
keyFacts: Bob pulls out two guns
Bob then grabs apartment tenant Hostage ... and forces him back toward the building
Get in here or I'll shoot you
issues.analysis: Bob seized Hostage by force and threat of a gun and moved him into the building (substantial movement increasing risk), and threatened to shoot; guilty of kidnapping (possibly aggravated), false imprisonment, assault/battery, and assault with a deadly weapon. No defenses.

issues.name: Bob – shooting at police (attempted murder / assault on officers)
issues.rule: Attempted murder requires specific intent to kill plus a direct act; firing a gun at persons supports an inference of intent to kill; alternatively assault with a firearm on a peace officer.
keyFacts: The police arrive, and Bob shoots at them
issues.analysis: Shooting at officers supports attempted murder of the police (or at minimum assault with a firearm on officers), with no self-defense or other justification as he is a felon resisting lawful arrest.

issues.name: Bob – murder liability for Hostage's death (felony murder / provocative act)
issues.rule: Felony murder: killing during commission or attempted commission of burglary, kidnapping, arson, etc. is murder; under the majority agency rule, felony murder does not apply when a non-felon (police, victim) fires the fatal shot, but the provocative act doctrine imposes murder liability when the defendant's life-threatening conduct (shooting at police, using a hostage) provokes a lethal response. Alternatively implied-malice (depraved heart) murder.
keyFacts: As Hostage is running from the building, he is shot and killed by the police who mistake him for a suspect
Bob shoots at the police
issues.analysis: The felonies were ongoing (no temporary safety reached), and Bob provoked the police response by shooting and taking Hostage, so the death was a foreseeable result; he is liable for murder (first-degree felony murder where kidnapping/burglary applies, or second-degree via provocative act/implied malice), though under a strict agency rule felony murder would fail. Fallback: involuntary manslaughter.

issues.name: Carl – conspiracy, burglary, larceny
issues.rule: Same elements as for Bob; each conspirator is liable for the agreed offenses, and Carl's own intent (he did not know of the bomb or guns) governs his own liability.
keyFacts: Bob and Carl break into GPC's headquarters and remove the model
Unknown to Al and Carl
Carl did not know
issues.analysis: Carl is guilty of conspiracy, burglary and larceny (subject to the same intent-to-permanently-deprive argument), but not of attempted arson since he did not know of the bomb.

issues.name: Carl – Pinkerton / accomplice liability for Bob's other crimes
issues.rule: A conspirator is liable under Pinkerton for crimes of co-conspirators that are reasonably foreseeable and in furtherance of the conspiracy; an accomplice is liable for crimes he aids with intent to facilitate and for natural and probable consequences of the target crime.
keyFacts: Unknown to Al and Carl, Bob intends to plant a bomb
Bob pulls out two guns (which Carl did not know Bob had) and tosses one to Carl
Carl pleads with Bob to let Hostage go
issues.analysis: The conspiracy was a nonviolent theft of a model (effigy), so the bomb, hostage-taking, kidnapping and shooting at police were not foreseeable and not in furtherance; Carl pleaded for release and did not shoot. Carl accepted a gun and followed Bob into the building, so the state may argue accomplice to kidnapping/assault, but intent to facilitate is lacking. Likely not liable for Bob's violent crimes.

issues.name: Carl – felony murder of Hostage
issues.rule: Felony murder attaches to a participant in an enumerated or inherently dangerous felony for any death proximately caused during the felony before reaching temporary safety, but the agency rule bars liability where the fatal shot was by a non-felon, and the killing must be in furtherance.
keyFacts: Hostage ... is shot and killed by the police who mistake him for a suspect
Carl finally convinces Bob to let Hostage go
issues.analysis: The burglary was in progress/escape, but the kidnapping was Bob's separate venture and police killed the victim; under the agency rule or lack of foreseeability Carl is probably not liable for murder; at most he faces involuntary manslaughter risk, which is weak. Close call dependent on jurisdiction.

issues.name: Carl – duress / withdrawal defenses
issues.rule: Duress requires a threat of imminent death or serious bodily injury that induces the crime, and is not a defense to murder; withdrawal requires timely communication and (in MPC) thwarting.
keyFacts: Get in here or I'll shoot you
Bob turns his back and takes Hostage into the building and Carl follows
Carl finally convinces Bob to let Hostage go
issues.analysis: The threat was directed at Hostage, not Carl, and Bob turned his back, so duress is weak (both students misread it as aimed at Carl); Carl's persuasion is mitigating, not withdrawal.

notes: Facts say Bob's 'Get in here or I'll shoot you' was to Hostage, not Carl; both students treated it as a threat to Carl. Felony-murder results turn on jurisdiction (agency rule vs. proximate cause); check how you want to treat California (People v. Washington agency rule plus provocative act doctrine). Student A says withdrawal bars liability for later crimes; Student B says it fails. Common law favors Student A for Pinkerton; MPC adds thwarting.
